result.question: What does Apple say about its dependence on third-party manufacturing and logistics partners?
result.answer:
Apple states that it depends on component and product manufacturing and logistical services provided by outsourcing partners, many of which are located outside of the U.S. [c1], [c3], [c4], [c5]

Substantially all (described as "a significant majority" in the 2025 10-K) of Apple's manufacturing is performed in whole or in part by outsourcing partners located primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam [c1], [c3], [c5]. A significant concentration of this manufacturing is performed by a small number of outsourcing partners, often in single locations [c1], [c3]. Apple relies on single-source outsourcing partners in the U.S., Asia and Europe to supply and manufacture many components, and on outsourcing partners primarily located in Asia for final assembly of substantially all of its hardware products [c2], [c3], [c5]. Any failure of these partners to perform can have a negative impact on Apple's cost or supply of components or finished goods [c2], [c3].

Apple has also outsourced much of its transportation and logistics management [c1], [c3], [c5]. While these arrangements can lower operating costs, they also reduce Apple's direct control over production and distribution [c1], [c3], [c5]. Such diminished control has from time to time had, and may in the future have, an adverse effect on the cost, quality or quantity of products manufactured or services provided, or adversely affect Apple's flexibility to respond to changing conditions [c1], [c3], [c5].

Although arrangements with these partners may contain provisions for product defect expense reimbursement, Apple generally remains responsible to the consumer for warranty and out-of-warranty service in the event of product defects and experiences unanticipated product defect liabilities from time to time [c1], [c3], [c5]. While Apple relies on its partners to adhere to its supplier code of conduct, violations occur from time to time and can materially adversely affect Apple's business, reputation, results of operations and financial condition [c1], [c3], [c5].

Apple has invested in manufacturing process equipment, much of which is held at certain of its outsourcing partners, and has made prepayments to certain suppliers associated with long-term supply agreements [c2], [c3]. If these outsourcing partners or suppliers experience severe financial problems or other disruptions, continued supply can be reduced, disrupted, or terminated, and the recoverability of manufacturing process equipment or prepayments can be negatively impacted [c2], [c3].

Changes or additions to Apple's supply chain require considerable time and resources and involve significant risks and uncertainties, including exposure to additional regulatory and operational risks [c1], [c4], [c5]. Manufacturing or logistics in these locations or transit to final destinations can be disrupted for a variety of reasons, including natural and man-made disasters, information technology system failures, commercial disputes, armed conflict, economic, business, labor, environmental, public health or political issues, trade and other international disputes, geopolitical tensions, or conflict [c2], [c3].
